newsitem.title: INDIA: India says "boom" could have come outside Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: India says "boom" could have come outside Pakistan.

text.p: India on Thursday denied that one of its jet fighters had violated Pakistan's airspace and said the sonic boom that shook Islamabad could have been produced by a plane outside of Pakistan's borders.
The Pakistan Air Force said a loud boom that rattled windows of buildings in Islamabad on Tuesday was caused by an Indian jet when it broke the sound barrier while flying out of Pakistani airspace.
Pakistan on Wednesday lodged a strong protest with India, saying the suspected intrusion violated international law and a bilateral agreement.
But New Delhi said no Indian aircraft had crossed the border.
"We deny any Indian aircraft, either civilian or military, crossed the international border," a Defence Ministry spokesman said.
The spokesman said a sonic boom can be heard from as far away as 120 km (75 miles), depending on the aircraft's speed, altitude and direction.
Islamabad is about 80 km (50 miles) from the line of control dividing Pakistan and the Indian region of Jammu.
"If a sonic boom occurs on this side of the border, it may be heard on the other side," the Defence Ministry spokesman said.
The spokesman, however, said he knew of no plane that broke the sonic boom in Indian airspace on Tuesday.
The incident echoed in the Pakistani parliament, reviving talk of rivalry between the two old enemies after a recent resumption of peace talks.
Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, speaking in the National Assembly, called the suspected intrusion serious and said it could have been made to photograph strategic installations.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, the last one in 1971, but recently resumed bilateral talks to normalise relations.
